header.title: Five steps from a clone to a place on the ladder
header.sub: Train a small neural network and submit it with a manifest that tells the referee how to talk to it. The platform weighs the pair into a weight class and starts playing it.

measured.heading: Your bytes set your class
measured.body: We measure what you submit: the graph's bytes plus the manifest's, against digests we re-hash. That number picks your class, and there you rank against competitors with the same budget. Each version also plays on Open, against models of any size.
measured.hint: Each season sets its own classes. [Measuring size](/docs/models/weight-classes)
measured.hintSeason: These are {game} {season}'s caps, and each season sets its own. [Measuring size](/docs/models/weight-classes)

items.value: The platform uses it to tell whose entry is whose, and signing in creates your account.
If you train the way the baselines do. Any tool that exports an ONNX graph works, and the format chapter lists the operators.
Playing the starter takes minutes, and retraining its entry about an hour that you can spend elsewhere. The manifest takes the most thought.

stages.title: The referee sends an observation
stages.said: Your living ants, and what they can see: enemy ants, food, hills, and the water found so far. Your model gets no score, no turn number and no memory between turns.

stages.title: Your model takes tensors
stages.said: The shapes your manifest declares. H and W may be names, so one manifest plays every board size.

stages.title: …and returns tensors
stages.said: Five scores per cell here, one per move. A per-ant graph returns [N, 5] instead.

stages.title: The referee gets one move per ant
stages.said: One of N E S W - for each ant, in order. The game fixes the channel order. The three steps share one turn’s deadline.

items.title: Clone the starter and play a match
paragraphs: ants-starter is a working entry you can submit unchanged: a trained nano model, its manifest, and the command that retrains it. It plays the ladder’s match on your own machine, with the same engine, boards and referee, and needs no Docker, database or account.
You install the tinybrains CLI with Homebrew or as a release binary. The starter pins the game to a release that the CLI downloads once, so you clone and build nothing else.
items.code:
# once
brew tap tiny-brains/cli https://github.com/Tiny-Brains/cli
brew install tiny-brains/cli/tinybrains
git clone https://github.com/Tiny-Brains/ants-starter
cd ants-starter && tinybrains matches/self-play.json
items.see: `300 turns, 600 seat-turns: mean 86063 ops, mean 2.46 ms inference`, a replay under `replays/` that `tinybrains view replays/self-play.json` plays, and ants that move.

docs.label: Match files: other boards, other opponents

items.title: Train something small
paragraphs: The starter’s train.py runs the recipe we trained the platform’s baselines with: a scripted teacher, behaviour cloning into a weight class, and an export that prints the platform’s verdict. It overwrites the entry at the top of the repository: model.onnx, manifest.json, metrics.json and card.md. Its nano entry is 3,006 parameters in 12 KiB.
Width, depth and fp16 each move the one number that decides your class. The smallest class has a ladder of its own, so a tiny model can top one.
items.code:
# collect, clone, export: about an hour
cd ants-starter && pip install -r requirements.txt
python train.py --seed 3
# a bigger class is the same recipe with a bigger budget
python train.py --class micro --skip-collect
items.see: Collecting takes about nine minutes and 90 MB. The export prints `12,280 bytes, 75% of the nano cap` and the inference time, and the two files it writes are the new version.

items.title: Write the manifest
paragraphs: manifest.json declares what your graph takes and returns, and carries one adapter expression per input: a small JSON program that turns the observation the referee sends into that tensor. A dimension may be a name: H and W bind to the board the season runs, so one manifest serves every size.

The manifest is data, so we measure it alongside the weights. You do not write the output side: the referee reads your policy head. The baselines generate their manifest from the code that trains them, so the two encodings cannot drift.
items.code:
// manifest.json — two planes in, a per-cell policy out
{ "abi": "orion:model@1.0.0", "format": "onnx", "name": "tb.mine",
  "inputs": [{ "name": "board", "dtype": "i8",
    "shape": [1, 2, "H", "W"],
    "adapter": { "reshape": [
      { "stack": [[ {"scatter": [{"var": "mine"}, {"var": "size"}, "i8"]},
                    {"rle_expand": [{"var": "water.rle"},
                                    {"var": "size"}, "i8"]} ], 0] },
      { "merge": [[1, 2], {"var": "size"}] } ] } }],
  "outputs": [{ "name": "policy", "dtype": "f32",
                "shape": [1, 5, "H", "W"] }],
  "probe_dims": { "H": 128, "W": 128 } }
items.see: `tinybrains adapt model.onnx manifest.json` writes the tensor each adapter builds for each of the ten reference observations, as `.npy` files. Compare them with your trainer’s encoder before you train on anything.

docs.label: A real manifest, piece by piece

items.title: Check it the way admission will
paragraphs: tinybrains check measures what admission measures, over the game’s reference observations. It reads the graph from the protobuf, evaluates the manifest on the expression engine a node uses, and runs the graph on the same runtime. It prints the operators, the size metric, the worst operation count against the budget, and the slowest inference. Then play the starter’s baseline match, which seats your model.onnx against the nano baseline.
A local pass does not guarantee admission, and admission alone decides your class.
items.code:
tinybrains check model.onnx manifest.json
# then play it against the nano baseline
tinybrains matches/vs-nano-bc.json
tinybrains view replays/vs-nano-bc.json
items.see: `adapters (10 reference observations, budget 1000000, turn 1000 ms) PASSED`, the worst case’s operations against the budget, and the slowest inference. Then a replay in which your ants move.

items.title: Submit and upload
paragraphs: Name your model once on Your models, then go to /submit and choose it and your two files. The page hashes them in your browser and uploads them to the object store, bypassing the site. You need no repository and cut no release.

This step has nothing to paste. To script it, use the two calls in the book. Either way, the platform re-hashes what arrives and refuses a file that differs from what you declared, naming the hash it measured.
items.code:
# nothing to run: /submit takes the two files
# scripting it instead? the digests it would declare are
shasum -a 256 model.onnx manifest.json # sha256sum on Linux
items.see: Both digests on screen as you pick, then **“Both files uploaded.”** Most verdicts reach the version page within minutes.

after.heading: After you submit
after.say: We check the files against the hashes you declared, measure them into a class, and play one trial against a baseline, which passes if it finishes under the strike limit, win or lose. Your version then plays without a break, and the previous one keeps playing until the new one is through. You get a notification at each step.

help.heading: Stuck?
help.body: Ask on Discord, where competitors and the people who run the platform talk. The source of the platform, the game and the tools is on GitHub.
